decks.title: Calorimetry — Part 1: Specific heat capacity and mixtures
goals: Distinguish heat from temperature and state their units
Use Q = mcΔT and relate heat capacity to specific heat capacity
Apply the principle of mixtures to find a final temperature or a specific heat capacity
Explain effects of the high specific heat capacity of water

slides.heading: Why is the sand hot and the sea cool?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — on a sunny afternoon the beach sand is too hot to walk on, yet the sea stays cool. Different materials need different amounts of heat to warm up.

visual.alt: Table of specific heat capacities of five substances

slides.narration: Namaste! On a hot day at the beach, the sand burns your feet but the sea feels cool, even though both receive the same sunshine. Water needs far more heat than sand to warm up by the same amount. In this part we measure this property, called specific heat capacity, and use it to predict temperatures when hot and cold things mix.

slides.heading: Heat and temperature
slides.body_md: **Heat** is a form of energy that flows from a hotter body to a colder one; SI unit **joule (J)**; also the **calorie** (1 cal ≈ 4.2 J), the heat needed to warm 1 g of water by 1 °C. **Temperature** is the degree of hotness that decides the direction of heat flow; SI unit **kelvin (K)**, commonly **degree Celsius (°C)**; a change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K. A bucket of warm water holds more heat than a cup of boiling water, though its temperature is lower.

visual.alt: Table comparing heat and temperature

slides.narration: Heat is energy that flows from a hotter body to a colder one, and it is measured in joules. Temperature tells us how hot something is, and it decides which way heat will flow; it is measured in kelvin or degrees Celsius. A bucket of warm water contains more heat energy than a cup of boiling water, even though its temperature is lower.

slides.heading: Heat capacity and specific heat capacity
slides.body_md: **Heat capacity** $C$ of a body: heat needed to raise its temperature by 1 °C (1 K); unit **J K⁻¹**. **Specific heat capacity** $c$ of a substance: heat needed to raise the temperature of **1 kg** of it by 1 K; unit **J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹** (also J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹). Relation: $C = mc$. Heat absorbed or given out: $Q = mc\,\Delta T$. Water has a very high value, $c = 4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}$ (4.2 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹).

visual.alt: Table comparing heat capacity and specific heat capacity

slides.narration: The heat capacity of a body is the heat needed to raise its temperature by one degree, and it depends on how much material there is. Specific heat capacity is the heat needed for one kilogram of a substance, so it depends only on what the substance is. Heat capacity equals mass times specific heat capacity, and the heat taken in is mass times specific heat capacity times the rise in temperature.

slides.heading: Worked example: using Q = mcΔT
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** How much heat is needed to warm 2 kg of water from 25 °C to 75 °C? What is the heat capacity of this water? ($c = 4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}$)

**Heat:** $Q = mc\,\Delta T = 2 \times 4200 \times 50 = 420000\ \text{J}$ ($420\ \text{kJ}$).

**Heat capacity:** $C = mc = 2 \times 4200 = 8400\ \text{J K}^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Table of values for heating two kilograms of water

slides.narration: Multiply mass, specific heat capacity and temperature rise: two times four thousand two hundred times fifty gives four hundred and twenty thousand joules. The heat capacity of this water is its mass times its specific heat capacity, eight thousand four hundred joules per kelvin, which is the heat needed for each one degree rise.

slides.heading: Quick check: specific heat capacity
slides.body_md: Calculate heat or compare specific heat capacities.
slides.narration: Quick check. Heat equals mass times specific heat capacity times temperature change.

slides.heading: Principle of method of mixtures
slides.body_md: When a hot body and a cold body are mixed and **no heat is lost to the surroundings**, **heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the cold body**, until both reach the same final temperature $T$. For a hot body (mass $m_1$, specific heat $c_1$, temperature $T_1$) and a cold one ($m_2$, $c_2$, $T_2$): $m_1c_1(T_1 - T) = m_2c_2(T - T_2)$. A **calorimeter** (a polished copper vessel in an insulating jacket, with a stirrer and thermometer) reduces heat loss.

slides.narration: When a hot object is put into cold water, heat flows from the hot object to the water until they reach the same temperature. If no heat escapes to the surroundings, the heat lost by the hot object equals the heat gained by the water. A calorimeter, a polished copper can kept in an insulating jacket, is used to keep heat losses small.

slides.heading: Worked example: mixing hot and cold water
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 0.5 kg of water at 80 °C is mixed with 1.5 kg of water at 20 °C. Find the final temperature, assuming no heat is lost.

**Heat lost** $= 0.5 \times c \times (80 - T)$; **heat gained** $= 1.5 \times c \times (T - 20)$.

Equate (the $c$ cancels): $40 - 0.5T = 1.5T - 30$, so $2T = 70$ and $T = 35\ ^\circ\text{C}$.

visual.alt: Table of the hot and cold water in the mixing example

slides.narration: Write heat lost equal to heat gained. Both are water, so the specific heat capacity cancels. Half a kilogram falls from eighty degrees to the final temperature, while one and a half kilograms rises from twenty. Solving gives thirty five degrees Celsius. Notice that the smaller hot mass changes temperature three times as much as the larger cold mass.

slides.heading: Worked example: specific heat capacity of a metal
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A 0.4 kg metal block at 100 °C is dropped into 0.6 kg of water at 25 °C. The final temperature is 30 °C. Ignoring the calorimeter, find the specific heat capacity of the metal.

**Heat gained by water** $= 0.6 \times 4200 \times 5 = 12600\ \text{J}$.

**Heat lost by metal** $= 0.4 \times c \times 70 = 28c$.

$28c = 12600$, so $c = 450\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}$, a value typical of iron or steel.

visual.alt: Table of heat gained by water and heat lost by the metal

slides.narration: The water warms by five degrees, so it gains twelve thousand six hundred joules. The metal cools by seventy degrees and must lose the same heat. Dividing twelve thousand six hundred by nought point four times seventy gives four hundred and fifty joules per kilogram per kelvin, a value typical of iron or steel.

slides.heading: Quick check: method of mixtures
slides.body_md: Find a final temperature by the method of mixtures.
slides.narration: Quick check. Heat lost by the hot body equals heat gained by the cold body.

slides.heading: Water’s high specific heat capacity
slides.body_md: Water warms up and cools down slowly because its specific heat capacity is very high. Effects and uses: **sea and land breezes**; **coastal places have a moderate climate**; **water as a coolant** in car radiators and power stations; **hot-water bottles** stay warm for long; **farmers flood fields** on frosty nights so the water gives out heat and protects crops; the **human body** (mostly water) resists sudden temperature changes.

slides.narration: Water has an unusually high specific heat capacity, so it heats and cools slowly. By day the land heats faster than the sea and a cool sea breeze blows inland; at night the land cools faster and a land breeze blows out to sea. Water is used to cool car engines and in hot water bottles, and farmers flood fields on frosty nights to protect their crops.

slides.heading: Quick check: uses of water
slides.body_md: Explain an effect of the high specific heat capacity of water.
slides.narration: Quick check. Water takes in or gives out a lot of heat for a small temperature change.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Heat: energy in transfer (J, cal); temperature: degree of hotness (K, °C).
Heat capacity C = mc (J K⁻¹); specific heat capacity c (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹); Q = mcΔT.
Method of mixtures: heat lost = heat gained (no loss to surroundings).
Water: c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; sea breezes, moderate coastal climate, coolant, hot-water bottles.

visual.alt: Summary table of formulae in Part 1

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Heat is energy in transfer and temperature is the degree of hotness. The heat to warm a body is mass times specific heat capacity times temperature rise. When things mix, heat lost equals heat gained. And because water has such a high specific heat capacity, it moderates climate and makes an excellent coolant.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Convert grams to kilograms when c is in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
In mixtures, write “heat lost = heat gained” and keep each ΔT positive.
Include the calorimeter’s heat if its mass and c are given.
State the assumption: no heat lost to the surroundings.

rows: Use (T₁ − T) for the hot body
Add m_cal c_cal ΔT when given

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some tips. Convert grams to kilograms when the specific heat capacity is per kilogram. In mixture problems, write heat lost equals heat gained and keep each temperature change positive. Include the calorimeter when its mass and specific heat are given. And state that no heat is lost to the surroundings.

decks.title: Calorimetry — Part 2: Change of state and latent heat of fusion
goals: Interpret the heating curve of ice to steam
Define specific latent heat of fusion and use Q = mL
Solve mixture problems involving melting ice
Explain everyday effects of the latent heat of fusion

slides.heading: Heat that does not raise the temperature
slides.body_md: Part 2 — when ice melts, it absorbs heat but its temperature stays at 0 °C until all of it has melted. Where does that heat go?

visual.alt: Table of four changes of state and whether heat is absorbed or given out

slides.narration: Put a thermometer in melting ice and keep heating it. The temperature stays at zero degrees until all the ice has gone, even though heat keeps flowing in. That heat is used to change solid ice into liquid water, not to make it hotter. In this part we measure this hidden or latent heat.

slides.heading: Change of state and latent heat
slides.body_md: A **change of state** (melting, boiling) happens at a **fixed temperature** for a pure substance at a given pressure. During melting, heat is absorbed to **separate the molecules from their fixed positions**, not to raise the temperature. **Specific latent heat of fusion** $L$: heat needed to change **1 kg** of a solid at its melting point into liquid at the same temperature; unit **J kg⁻¹**. For ice, $L = 336000\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$ (336 J g⁻¹). Heat to melt mass $m$: $Q = mL$. The same heat is **given out** when the liquid freezes.

rows: Specific latent heat of fusion of ice

visual.alt: Table of the two heat formulae and the latent heat of fusion of ice

slides.narration: A pure substance melts at a fixed temperature. While it melts, the heat it absorbs breaks the molecules free from their fixed positions instead of making it hotter. The heat needed to melt one kilogram at its melting point is called the specific latent heat of fusion. For ice it is three hundred and thirty six thousand joules per kilogram. When water freezes, the same heat is given out.

slides.heading: Heating curve of ice to steam
slides.body_md: Heating 1 kg of ice from −10 °C at a steady 1000 W: **AB** ice warms to 0 °C ($Q = mc_{\text{ice}}\Delta T$, 21 s); **BC** ice melts at 0 °C ($Q = mL$, 336 s) — flat; **CD** water warms to 100 °C ($Q = mc_{\text{water}}\Delta T$, 420 s); **DE** water boils at 100 °C — flat. The flat parts show **latent heat**: heat absorbed with no change in temperature. The melting part is much longer than the ice-warming part.

series.label: 1 kg of ice at −10 °C heated steadily

visual.alt: Heating curve of one kilogram of ice heated at a steady one kilowatt: the temperature rises from minus ten to zero degrees in 21 seconds, stays at zero for 336 seconds while the ice melts, rises to one hundred degrees in the next 420 seconds, and then stays at one hundred while the water boils
visual.caption: Flat parts: change of state at constant temperature (latent heat). Sloping parts: temperature rise (Q = mcΔT).

slides.narration: This graph shows one kilogram of ice heated steadily. First the ice warms from minus ten to zero degrees. Then the line is flat while the ice melts, for over five minutes, because all the heat goes into melting. Then the water warms up to one hundred degrees, and the line is flat again while it boils. The flat parts are where latent heat is absorbed.

slides.heading: Quick check: the heating curve
slides.body_md: Read the flat and sloping parts of a heating curve.
slides.narration: Quick check. Flat parts mean a change of state at constant temperature.

slides.heading: Worked example: melting ice
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** (a) How much heat is needed to melt 250 g of ice at 0 °C? (b) How much more to warm the melted water to 30 °C? ($L = 336000\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$, $c = 4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}$)

**(a)** $Q_1 = mL = 0.25 \times 336000 = 84000\ \text{J}$.

**(b)** $Q_2 = mc\,\Delta T = 0.25 \times 4200 \times 30 = 31500\ \text{J}$.

**Total** $= 115500\ \text{J}$.

visual.alt: Flow of heat needed to melt ice and then warm the water

slides.narration: Melting needs mass times latent heat: a quarter of a kilogram times three hundred and thirty six thousand gives eighty four thousand joules. Warming the melted water by thirty degrees needs mass times specific heat times temperature rise, thirty one thousand five hundred joules. Melting takes much more heat than warming, even for a thirty degree rise.

slides.heading: Quick check: latent heat
slides.body_md: Calculate the heat needed to melt ice.
slides.narration: Quick check. Heat to melt equals mass times specific latent heat of fusion.

slides.heading: Worked example: ice in a drink
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 50 g of ice at 0 °C is added to 200 g of water at 40 °C. Find the final temperature $T$, assuming no heat loss.

**Heat gained by ice:** melting $0.05 \times 336000 = 16800\ \text{J}$, then warming $0.05 \times 4200 \times T = 210T$.

**Heat lost by water:** $0.2 \times 4200 \times (40 - T) = 33600 - 840T$.

**Equate:** $16800 + 210T = 33600 - 840T$, so $1050T = 16800$ and $T = 16\ ^\circ\text{C}$.

visual.alt: Table of the heat terms in the ice-in-water example

slides.narration: The ice gains heat twice: first to melt, sixteen thousand eight hundred joules, then to warm the melted water up to the final temperature. The warm water loses heat as it cools from forty degrees. Setting heat gained equal to heat lost and solving gives a final temperature of sixteen degrees Celsius.

slides.heading: Worked example: heat given out on freezing
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** An ice tray holds 0.15 kg of water at 20 °C. How much heat must the freezer remove to turn it into ice at 0 °C?

**Cooling the water to 0 °C:** $Q_1 = mc\,\Delta T = 0.15 \times 4200 \times 20 = 12600\ \text{J}$.

**Freezing at 0 °C:** $Q_2 = mL = 0.15 \times 336000 = 50400\ \text{J}$.

**Total removed** $= 63000\ \text{J}$ — most of it latent heat.

visual.alt: Table of heat removed in cooling and freezing water in an ice tray

slides.narration: First the freezer must cool the water from twenty degrees down to zero, removing about twelve thousand six hundred joules. Then it must remove the latent heat, fifty thousand four hundred joules, to turn the water into ice at zero degrees. Freezing takes four times as much heat as the cooling, which is why ice trays take a long time to freeze.

slides.heading: Ice at 0 °C cools better than water at 0 °C
slides.body_md: Each kilogram of ice at 0 °C must **first absorb 336 000 J to melt** before it can warm up, while water at 0 °C starts warming at once. So ice takes much more heat from a drink: it cools better. Other effects of the latent heat of fusion: **snow on hills melts slowly**, keeping rivers flowing through summer; **frozen lakes thaw slowly**; ponds freeze slowly, because a lot of heat must be removed from the water before it turns to ice; **ice-cream** and **frozen foods** stay cold for long.

headers: Heat it can absorb before reaching 10 °C (per kg)

visual.alt: Table comparing the heat absorbed by water at zero degrees and ice at zero degrees in warming to ten degrees

slides.narration: Ice at zero degrees cools a drink much better than ice-cold water at zero degrees. Before the ice can even start to warm up, every kilogram must take in three hundred and thirty six thousand joules to melt, and that heat comes from the drink. Latent heat also explains why snow on mountains melts slowly through the summer, keeping rivers flowing.

slides.heading: Quick check: everyday latent heat
slides.body_md: Explain an everyday effect of latent heat of fusion.
slides.narration: Quick check. Ice must absorb its latent heat before its temperature can rise.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Change of state happens at constant temperature; heat goes into separating molecules.
Specific latent heat of fusion L: heat to melt 1 kg at its melting point; ice 336 000 J kg⁻¹; Q = mL.
Heating curve: sloping parts Q = mcΔT, flat parts Q = mL.
Ice at 0 °C cools better than water at 0 °C; snow and frozen lakes melt slowly.

visual.alt: Summary table of heating curve parts

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. A pure substance changes state at a fixed temperature, and the heat absorbed, the latent heat, does not raise its temperature. To melt a mass of ice takes mass times three hundred and thirty six thousand joules per kilogram. On a heating curve, the flat parts are changes of state. That is why ice at zero cools a drink better than water at zero.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Write separate terms: melting (mL) and then warming (mcΔT) of the melted ice.
Latent heat of fusion of ice: 336 J g⁻¹ = 336 000 J kg⁻¹ — keep units consistent.
Explain flat parts of a heating curve as “change of state at constant temperature”.
Only fusion numericals are examined; vaporisation is qualitative.

rows: Forgetting to warm the melted ice
Add m c T for it

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 2 and their fixes

slides.narration: Final tips. When ice is added to warm water, remember two steps for the ice: melting, then warming the melted water. Keep your units consistent, grams with joules per gram, or kilograms with joules per kilogram. Describe the flat parts of a heating curve as changes of state at constant temperature. Only latent heat of fusion is examined with numbers.

notes.title: Calorimetry — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Heat, temperature, heat capacity and specific heat capacity
sections.body_md:
- **Heat:** energy flowing from hot to cold; unit J (1 cal ≈ 4.2 J). **Temperature:** degree of hotness; unit K (°C in practice; a change of 1 °C = 1 K).
- **Heat capacity** $C$: heat to raise the temperature of a body by 1 K; unit J K⁻¹; depends on mass and material.
- **Specific heat capacity** $c$: heat to raise 1 kg by 1 K; unit J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; depends only on material. Water 4200, ice 2100, aluminium 900, copper 400.
- $C = mc$; $Q = mc\,\Delta T$.

key_terms.definition_md: The heat required to raise the temperature of a body by one kelvin.
The heat required to raise the temperature of unit mass of a substance by one kelvin.

visual.alt: Table of specific heat capacities

sections.heading: 2. Method of mixtures
sections.body_md:
**Principle:** when hot and cold bodies are mixed and no heat is lost to the surroundings, heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the cold body.

$m_1 c_1 (T_1 - T) = m_2 c_2 (T - T_2)$ (+ $m_{cal} c_{cal} (T - T_2)$ for the calorimeter).

A calorimeter is a thin polished copper vessel (low heat capacity, good conductor, polished to reduce radiation) in an insulating jacket, with stirrer and thermometer.

key_terms.definition_md: Heat lost by the hot body equals heat gained by the cold body, provided no heat is exchanged with the surroundings.
A vessel, usually of polished copper in an insulating jacket, used to measure heat exchanged.

visual.alt: Table of the two sides of a mixture

sections.heading: 3. High specific heat capacity of water
sections.body_md:
Water warms and cools slowly. Consequences and uses:
- **Sea breeze** by day (land hotter), **land breeze** at night (sea warmer).
- Coastal climates are moderate; inland deserts have extreme days and nights.
- **Coolant** in car radiators, power stations; **hot-water bottles**.
- **Farmers flood fields** on frosty nights; water gives out heat as it cools.
- Body temperature stays steady (body is mostly water).

key_terms.definition_md: A cool daytime wind blowing from the sea to the land, because land heats faster than water.

visual.alt: Table of effects of water’s high specific heat capacity

sections.heading: 4. Change of state and latent heat of fusion
sections.body_md:
A pure substance changes state at a fixed temperature (ice melts at 0 °C at normal pressure). Heat absorbed during melting separates the molecules and does not raise the temperature.

**Specific latent heat of fusion** $L$: heat to change 1 kg of solid at its melting point into liquid at the same temperature. Ice: $L = 336\,000\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$ (336 J g⁻¹). $Q = mL$.

**Heating curve** (ice → steam): sloping parts $Q = mc\Delta T$; flat parts at 0 °C (melting) and 100 °C (boiling) are latent heat.

key_terms.definition_md: The heat required to convert unit mass of a solid at its melting point into liquid at the same temperature.
The fixed temperature at which a pure solid changes into liquid at a given pressure.

visual.alt: Table of heating curve parts and formulae

sections.heading: 5. Everyday effects of latent heat of fusion
sections.body_md:
- **Ice at 0 °C cools better than water at 0 °C:** each kilogram absorbs 336 000 J to melt before warming.
- **Snow on mountains melts slowly**, so rivers keep flowing in summer.
- **Ponds and lakes freeze slowly**: a lot of heat must be removed first.
- **Frozen food and ice-cream** stay cold longer.
- Freezing water gives out heat: trays of water in a cellar protect stored vegetables from frost.

key_terms.definition_md: Heat absorbed or given out during a change of state without any change in temperature.

headers: Heat absorbed per kg before warming

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using grams with c in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
- Forgetting to warm the melted ice after it melts.
- Saying temperature rises while ice melts.
- Mixing up heat capacity (J K⁻¹) and specific heat capacity (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Mixture problems (3–4 marks): heat lost written, heat gained written, equation, answer with unit.
- Explanations (1–2 marks): name specific heat capacity or latent heat and say what it does.

questions.stem_md: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 500 g of water in a kettle from 20 °C to 50 °C?
The SI unit of specific heat capacity is:
questions.solution_md: Heat per unit mass per kelvin — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A bathtub of warm water at 40 °C and a cup of tea at 90 °C are compared. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: The tea is at a higher temperature, but the bathtub water contains more heat energy
The tea contains more heat because it is hotter
The bathtub water is at the higher temperature

questions.solution_md: Heat depends on mass as well as temperature — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A 0.5 kg aluminium pan (c = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) absorbs 18 000 J of heat. Its temperature rises by:
What is the heat capacity, in J K⁻¹, of a 2 kg copper block? (c of copper = 400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Find the heat (in J) needed to bring 1.5 kg of water from 25 °C to its boiling point 100 °C.
A 200 g block of an unknown metal absorbs 7200 J and warms by 40 °C. Find its specific heat capacity in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

**Assertion (A):** A large iron pot has a greater heat capacity than a small iron spoon.

**Reason (R):** Heat capacity depends on the mass of the body as well as on the material.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A (C = mc) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Specific heat capacity of a substance depends on the mass of the sample.
questions.solution_md: False: it is a property of the material; heat capacity depends on mass.

questions.stem_md: Heat capacity = mass × specific heat ___.
The SI unit of temperature is the ___.
Define specific heat capacity.

answer.model_answer_md: The heat needed to raise the temperature of unit mass (1 kg) of a substance through 1 K (1 °C).

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between heat capacity and specific heat capacity, giving the SI unit of each.

answer.model_answer_md: Heat capacity: heat needed to raise the temperature of a whole body by 1 K; depends on mass and material; unit J K⁻¹. Specific heat capacity: heat needed for 1 kg of a substance per 1 K; depends only on the material; unit J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: Whole body vs unit mass; units.

questions.stem_md: An aluminium pan of mass 0.8 kg contains 1.2 kg of water at 30 °C. Both are heated to 90 °C. (c of aluminium = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.) Calculate (a) the heat taken by the pan, (b) the heat taken by the water and (c) the total heat supplied.
300 g of water at 90 °C is poured into 600 g of water at 30 °C. Ignoring heat losses, the final temperature is:
The principle of the method of mixtures assumes that:

options.text_md: the two bodies have the same specific heat capacity
no heat is exchanged with the surroundings
the two bodies have equal masses
the final temperature is the average of the two

questions.solution_md: Only then is heat lost = heat gained — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A 200 g copper ball at 100 °C is dropped into 500 g of water at 20 °C (c of copper = 400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; ignore the container). The final temperature is about:
To prepare a bath, 2 kg of water at 70 °C is mixed with 3 kg of water at 20 °C. Find the final temperature in °C (no heat loss).

A 0.2 kg piece of metal at 100 °C is placed in 0.4 kg of water at 20 °C. The final temperature is 26 °C. Neglecting the container, find the specific heat capacity of the metal in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (to 3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Heat gained by water $= 0.4 \times 4200 \times 6 = 10080$ J; heat lost by metal $= 0.2 \times c \times 74$; so $c = 10080 \div 14.8 \approx 681$ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When equal masses of water at 20 °C and 80 °C are mixed, the final temperature is 50 °C.

**Reason (R):** Heat lost by the hot water equals heat gained by the cold water, and both have the same specific heat capacity.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A calorimeter is usually made of copper because copper has a high specific heat capacity.
questions.solution_md: False: copper is used because it is a good conductor with a low specific heat capacity, so it takes little of the heat.

questions.stem_md: In the method of mixtures, heat lost by the hot body = heat ___ by the cold body.
State the principle of the method of mixtures.

answer.model_answer_md: If no heat is exchanged with the surroundings, the heat lost by the hot body is equal to the heat gained by the cold body.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why a calorimeter is made of thin, polished copper and kept in an insulating jacket.

answer.model_answer_md: Copper is a good conductor with a low specific heat capacity, so the vessel quickly reaches the mixture’s temperature and takes little heat; polishing (and the insulating jacket) reduces heat loss by radiation and by conduction and convection to the surroundings.

questions.solution_md: Low c, good conductor; reduced losses.

questions.stem_md: A 100 g iron nail (c = 500 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 100 °C is dropped into a 100 g copper calorimeter (c = 400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) containing 300 g of water at 20 °C. Write the heat-balance equation and find the final temperature to one decimal place.

answer.model_answer_md: Heat lost by nail $= 0.1 \times 500 \times (100 - T)$; heat gained $= (0.3 \times 4200 + 0.1 \times 400)(T - 20)$. So $50(100 - T) = 1300(T - 20)$, giving $1350T = 31000$ and $T \approx 23$ °C.

questions.stem_md: Coastal towns such as Mumbai have a smaller difference between day and night temperatures than inland deserts such as Jaisalmer. This is mainly because:

options.text_md: sand has a high specific heat capacity
the sea has a high specific heat capacity, so it warms and cools slowly
water has a low specific heat capacity

questions.solution_md: Water moderates the temperature of nearby land — option (b).

questions.stem_md: On a sunny afternoon at the seaside, the breeze at ground level blows:

options.text_md: from the sea to the land, because the land heats up faster
from the land to the sea, because the sea heats up faster
from the land to the sea, because the land heats up faster

questions.solution_md: Warm air rises over the land and cooler sea air flows in — option (a).

questions.stem_md: On frosty nights, farmers in Himachal sometimes flood their fields with water. This protects the crops because:

options.text_md: water gives out a lot of heat as it cools, keeping the field warmer
water has a low specific heat capacity
water absorbs heat from the crops
water stops all air from reaching the crops

questions.solution_md: High c: much heat released per degree of cooling — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Water is used as a coolant in car radiators.

**Reason (R):** Water has a low specific heat capacity, so it heats up quickly.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true; R is false: water has a high specific heat capacity, so it absorbs much heat for a small rise — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A hot-water bottle stays warm for a long time because water has a high specific heat capacity.
questions.solution_md: True: it releases a lot of heat for each degree it cools.

questions.stem_md: Explain why (a) a sea breeze blows during the day and (b) water is used in hot-water bottles.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Land has a much lower specific heat capacity than sea water, so by day it heats faster; warm air above the land rises and cooler air from the sea flows in. (b) Water has a high specific heat capacity, so it gives out a large amount of heat as it cools, keeping the bottle warm for long.

questions.stem_md: How much heat is needed to melt 150 g of ice at 0 °C into water at 0 °C?
On the heating curve of ice heated steadily, the temperature stays at 0 °C for some time because:

options.text_md: ice has a very low specific heat capacity
heat is lost to the surroundings at exactly the same rate
the heat supplied is used to change ice into water, not to raise the temperature

questions.solution_md: Latent heat of fusion is absorbed — option (d).

questions.stem_md: On the heating curve of 1 kg of ice from −10 °C at constant power, the melting part (at 0 °C) is much longer than the ice-warming part because:

options.text_md: melting 1 kg needs 336 000 J, while warming the ice by 10 °C needs only 21 000 J
ice has a higher specific heat capacity than water
the heater power falls during melting

questions.stem_md: A freezer removes 168 000 J of heat from water at 0 °C. What mass of ice (in kg) is formed?
Find the total heat (in J) needed to change 200 g of ice at −5 °C into water at 0 °C. (c of ice = 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; L = 336 000 J kg⁻¹)
questions.solution_md: Warm the ice: $0.2 \times 2100 \times 5 = 2100$ J; melt it: $0.2 \times 336000 = 67200$ J; total $= 69300$ J.

questions.stem_md: 60 g of ice at 0 °C is added to 300 g of lemonade (treat as water) at 50 °C. Find the final temperature in °C, to one decimal place, assuming no heat loss.

**Assertion (A):** The temperature of a mixture of ice and water stays at 0 °C while it is being heated, until all the ice melts.

**Reason (R):** Heat absorbed during melting is used to overcome the forces holding the molecules in fixed positions.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Water at 0 °C gives out heat when it freezes into ice at 0 °C.
questions.solution_md: True: it gives out its latent heat of fusion.

questions.stem_md: The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 336 ___ (unit, per gram). (Write the unit symbol.)
Define specific latent heat of fusion.

answer.model_answer_md: The heat energy needed to change unit mass (1 kg) of a solid at its melting point into liquid at the same temperature.

questions.stem_md: Sketch (or describe) the heating curve of ice at −10 °C heated until it is water at 100 °C, labelling the part where latent heat is absorbed.

answer.model_answer_md: Temperature rises from −10 °C to 0 °C (ice warming); stays constant at 0 °C for a long time (ice melting — latent heat of fusion absorbed); then rises steadily from 0 °C to 100 °C (water warming).

marking_scheme.step: Flat part labelled as latent heat

questions.stem_md: Ice at 0 °C cools a glass of juice more than the same mass of ice-cold water at 0 °C because:

options.text_md: ice is colder than water at 0 °C
each gram of ice must absorb 336 J from the juice just to melt
ice has a higher specific heat capacity than water
water at 0 °C gives heat to the juice

questions.solution_md: Latent heat of fusion is taken from the juice — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Snow on the Himalayas melts slowly through summer, so the Ganga keeps flowing. This is because:

options.text_md: snow has a high melting point
snow has a low specific heat capacity
snow needs a large amount of latent heat to melt

questions.solution_md: Large L means slow melting for the heat received — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A tub of water kept in a cellar on a freezing night helps protect stored vegetables, because the water gives out latent heat as it freezes.
Heat absorbed during melting without any rise in temperature is called latent heat of ___.
Show by calculation how much more heat 100 g of ice at 0 °C can take from a drink, compared with 100 g of water at 0 °C, before each reaches 0 °C as water.

answer.model_answer_md: Ice must melt first: $Q = mL = 0.1 \times 336000 = 33600$ J; water at 0 °C is already liquid and absorbs nothing to reach the same state. So the ice takes 33600 J more.

questions.stem_md: The heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of water by 1 °C is:
1 kg of dry sand (c = 840 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) and 1 kg of sea water (c ≈ 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) each absorb the same heat from the Sun. The sand warms up:

options.text_md: about five times as much as the water

questions.stem_md: How much heat (in J) is given out when 3 kg of water cools from 80 °C to 30 °C?
A hair-dryer supplies 25 200 J of heat to a block of ice at 0 °C. What mass of ice (in kg) melts?
True or false? While pure water is boiling at normal pressure, its temperature keeps rising as heat is supplied.
questions.solution_md: False: it stays at 100 °C; the heat is used to change the state.

questions.stem_md: At normal atmospheric pressure, pure ice melts at ___ °C.
Explain why (a) a pond takes a long time to freeze completely in winter and (b) a tub of water kept beside stored vegetables protects them on a frosty night.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Before the water can turn to ice, a large amount of latent heat of fusion (336 J for every gram) must be removed from it, so freezing is slow. (b) As the water freezes it gives out its latent heat of fusion to the surroundings, keeping the air near the vegetables from falling much below 0 °C.

questions.solution_md: Latent heat removed slowly; latent heat released.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A lump of ice at 0 °C feels colder to the touch than water at 0 °C.

**Reason (R):** Melting ice absorbs latent heat from the hand.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Write the formula for the heat absorbed by a body of mass m and specific heat capacity c when its temperature rises by ΔT.
Match each quantity in Column A with its SI unit in Column B.
questions.solution_md: Heat → J; heat capacity → J K⁻¹; specific heat capacity → J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; specific latent heat → J kg⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: Match each observation in Column A with its explanation in Column B.

match_right.text_md: Land heats faster than the sea

questions.solution_md: Sea breeze → land heats faster; radiator → high c; ice cools drinks → latent heat; flat curve → change of state.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between heat and temperature, giving the SI unit of each. [3]

(b) Define specific heat capacity and write the relation between heat capacity and specific heat capacity. Calculate the heat capacity of 3 kg of water. [3]

(c) A 250 g copper block (c = 400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 150 °C is dropped into 500 g of water at 25 °C in an insulated container of negligible heat capacity. (i) Write the heat-balance equation. (ii) Find the final temperature to one decimal place. (iii) State the principle used. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Heat is energy that flows from a hotter to a colder body (unit joule); temperature is the degree of hotness that decides the direction of heat flow (unit kelvin).

(b) Heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K. $C = mc$; $C = 3 \times 4200 = 12600$ J K⁻¹.

(c) (i) $0.25 \times 400 \times (150 - T) = 0.5 \times 4200 \times (T - 25)$. (ii) $100(150 - T) = 2100(T - 25)$, so $2200T = 67500$ and $T \approx 30.7$ °C. (iii) Principle of method of mixtures: heat lost = heat gained when no heat is lost to the surroundings.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the principle of the method of mixtures and the condition for it to hold. [3]

(b) Why is a calorimeter (i) made of copper, (ii) polished and (iii) kept in a wooden box or insulating jacket? [3]

(c) A 200 g metal block at 100 °C is put into a 100 g copper calorimeter (c = 400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) containing 500 g of water at 20 °C. The final temperature is 24 °C. (i) Find the heat gained by the water. (ii) Find the heat gained by the calorimeter. (iii) Find the specific heat capacity of the metal to 3 significant figures. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the cold body, provided no heat is exchanged with the surroundings.

(b) (i) Good conductor with low specific heat capacity, so it quickly takes the mixture’s temperature and absorbs little heat. (ii) To reduce heat loss by radiation. (iii) To reduce loss by conduction and convection.

(c) (i) $0.5 \times 4200 \times 4 = 8400$ J. (ii) $0.1 \times 400 \times 4 = 160$ J. (iii) Heat lost by metal $= 0.2 \times c \times 76 = 8560$ J, so $c \approx 563$ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: Principle; calorimeter design; specific heat of metal.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Water has a high specific heat capacity. Explain how this causes (i) sea breezes by day and (ii) land breezes at night. [3]

(b) Give three other uses or effects of the high specific heat capacity of water. [3]

(c) Equal masses (1 kg) of water and sand each receive 42 000 J. (c of sand = 840 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.) (i) Find the rise in temperature of each. (ii) Which gets hotter and by how many times? (iii) Relate this to a beach on a sunny day. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) By day, land (low c) heats faster than the sea; hot air over land rises and cooler air from the sea blows in at the surface. (ii) At night land cools faster; the sea is warmer, air rises over the sea and air from the land blows towards it.

(b) Any three: coolant in car radiators; hot-water bottles; farmers flood fields on frosty nights; coastal climates are moderate; body temperature stays steady.

(c) (i) Water: $42000 \div (1 \times 4200) = 10$ °C. Sand: $42000 \div (1 \times 840) = 50$ °C. (ii) Sand, 5 times as much. (iii) On a sunny day the sand becomes far hotter than the sea water.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by latent heat? Define specific latent heat of fusion and state its value for ice. [3]

(b) 500 g of ice at −10 °C is heated until it becomes water at 100 °C. (c of ice = 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.) Calculate the heat needed (i) to warm the ice to 0 °C, (ii) to melt it and (iii) to warm the water to 100 °C. [3]

(c) (i) Sketch the temperature–time graph for (b) at constant heater power. (ii) Which stage takes the longest? (iii) Why is the temperature constant during melting? (iv) Find the total heat. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Heat absorbed or given out during a change of state without a change of temperature. Specific latent heat of fusion: heat needed to change 1 kg of solid at its melting point into liquid at the same temperature; for ice 336 000 J kg⁻¹.

(b) (i) $0.5 \times 2100 \times 10 = 10500$ J. (ii) $0.5 \times 336000 = 168000$ J. (iii) $0.5 \times 4200 \times 100 = 210000$ J.

(c) (i) Rise from −10 °C to 0 °C; flat at 0 °C; rise to 100 °C. (ii) Warming the water (210000 J), slightly more than melting (168000 J). (iii) The heat is used to change the state (separate the molecules), not to raise the temperature. (iv) $10500 + 168000 + 210000 = 388500$ J.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain why ice at 0 °C is a better coolant than water at 0 °C. [3]

(b) Give two natural phenomena explained by the large latent heat of fusion of ice. [3]

(c) What mass of ice at 0 °C must be added to 400 g of water at 50 °C so that the final temperature is 10 °C? (i) Write the heat lost by the water. (ii) Write the heat gained by the ice in terms of its mass m. (iii) Solve for m in grams (to 3 significant figures). [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Each kilogram of ice must first absorb 336 000 J of latent heat to melt, at 0 °C, before its temperature can rise; water at 0 °C absorbs only mcΔT. So ice removes far more heat from the drink.

(b) Snow on mountains melts slowly, keeping rivers flowing; ponds and lakes freeze slowly in winter (also ice-cream and frozen food stay cold for long).

(c) (i) $0.4 \times 4200 \times (50 - 10) = 67200$ J. (ii) $m \times 336000 + m \times 4200 \times 10 = 378000\,m$. (iii) $m = 67200 \div 378000 \approx 0.178$ kg $\approx 178$ g.
